entities.name: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The oldest and longest of the principal Upanishads (c. 700 BCE), embedded within the Shatapatha Brahmana of the Shukla Yajurveda. It contains some of the most profound philosophical dialogues in Indian literature, centered on the sage Yajnavalkya's teachings to King Janaka and his wife Maitreyi. Key doctrines include: the identity of Atman (individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) — encapsulated in the mahavakya "Aham Brahmasmi" ("I am Brahman"); the nature of consciousness; the process of death and transmigration; and the path to moksha (liberation).

The Brihadaranyaka, along with the Chandogya Upanishad, forms the foundation of Vedanta philosophy — the dominant school of Hindu thought for over 2,000 years.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's teachings on the identity of Atman and Brahman have had a profound impact on Hindu thought for over 2,000 years, shaping the foundation of Vedanta philosophy. Its influence can be seen in various schools of Hinduism and has contributed to the development of Indian spirituality.
